country.name: China
country.tagline: The world's third-largest vineyard and its oldest fermented drink, now remaking itself from the desert edge of the Helan Mountains.

stats.note: OIV (May 2026): 733 kha of vineyard (third in the world, most of it table grapes and raisins) and 2.2 mhl of wine in 2025, down 17.8 percent on 2024 and ranked 18th; China was the fifth-largest producer at its 2012 peak.

country.overview:
China has the oldest chemical evidence of a fermented drink containing grapes and one of the youngest modern wine industries. At Jiahu, a Neolithic village in Henan, residues in pottery jars from about 7000 BC point to a mixed drink of rice, honey and fruit (hawthorn or wild grape). Grape wine proper arrived along the Silk Road: the Han envoy Zhang Qian travelled to Dayuan (Ferghana, in modern Uzbekistan) in the 130s and 120s BC, and by the end of the century Han envoys had brought grape seeds back to plant near the capital, Chang'an. Under the Tang, after the conquest of Gaochang near Turpan in 641, the court learned a 'method of wine making' and planted the long 'mare's teat' grape; poets such as Wang Han wrote of 'fine grape wine in luminous cups of jade'. Yet for most of Chinese history, grain-based huangjiu and later baijiu dominated, and grape wine stayed exotic.

Modern Chinese wine began in 1892, when Zhang Bishi, a Hakka tycoon from the Dutch East Indies, founded Changyu in the treaty port of Yantai, Shandong, and imported European vines (including the grape later identified as Carmenère and sold as 'Cabernet Gernischt'). The state-led era brought Great Wall (1983, at Shacheng in Hebei, now part of COFCO) and the Sino-French joint venture Dynasty (1980, with Rémy Martin, in Tianjin). These three dominated for decades, often blending imported bulk wine with local juice.

The 2000s and early 2010s saw a boom. Rising wealth made Bordeaux a status symbol, and China briefly became the world's biggest market for red wine; domestic production peaked in 2012, when China was the fifth-largest producer. Provincial governments, above all Ningxia's, poured money into new estates. Helan Qingxue's Jiabeilan 2009 won a Decanter international trophy in 2011, and Ningxia became the face of quality Chinese wine. LVMH's Moët Hennessy set up Chandon in Ningxia (2013) and the high-altitude Ao Yun estate in Yunnan (first vintage 2013), and Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite) planted Long Dai in Shandong.

The years since have been tough. An anti-corruption campaign from 2012 cut banquet and gift spending, consumption fell, and production dropped from more than 13 million hectolitres at its 2012 peak to 2.2 million in 2025. China's vineyard, the third-largest in the world at 733,000 ha, is now overwhelmingly for table grapes and raisins. But the quality end is better than ever: small estates in Ningxia, Xinjiang, Shandong, Hebei and Yunnan make serious Cabernet, Marselan and Chardonnay, and Ningxia hosted the 46th OIV World Congress in October 2026.

Viticulture in much of China is extreme. In the north and west, winters fall to minus 20 to minus 30 degrees C, so vines in Ningxia, Xinjiang, Gansu and Hebei must be buried under soil every November and dug out in April, an enormous labour cost that limits vine age and trunk size. In the east, summer monsoon rain brings rot and mildew. The best regions are those in the dry west with access to irrigation, or high mountain valleys in the south-west where the monsoon is blocked.

history.title: Jiahu fermented drink
history.text: Residues in pottery jars from the Neolithic village of Jiahu in Henan, analysed by Patrick McGovern and colleagues in 2004, revealed a fermented beverage of rice, honey and fruit (hawthorn and/or wild grape): the oldest chemically confirmed alcoholic drink in the world.

history.title: Zhang Qian reaches Ferghana
history.text: The Han envoy Zhang Qian reached Dayuan (Ferghana), whose people made and stored grape wine. Han envoys later brought grape seeds back to plant on imperial land near Chang'an.

history.title: Tang conquest of Gaochang
history.text: After conquering Gaochang, an oasis kingdom near Turpan, the Tang court acquired the 'mare's teat' grape and a method of winemaking. Tang poets such as Wang Han celebrated grape wine 'in luminous cups'.

history.title: Changyu at Yantai
history.text: Zhang Bishi founded Changyu in Yantai, Shandong, importing European vines; his Grand Cellar (1894 onward) still stands beside the sea. Changyu is the oldest and largest Chinese wine company.

history.title: Dynasty and Great Wall
history.text: Rémy Martin and Tianjin created Dynasty, China's first Sino-foreign wine joint venture, in 1980; the state-owned Great Wall winery was founded at Shacheng, Hebei, in 1983. With Changyu they dominated Chinese wine for 30 years.

history.title: Sino-French demonstration vineyard
history.text: A Sino-French demonstration vineyard planted at Donghuayuan in Huailai county, Hebei (now Domaine Franco-Chinois), introduced varieties including Marselan, which became a Chinese specialty.

history.title: Ningxia's Decanter trophy
history.text: Helan Qingxue's Jiabeilan 2009, made by consultant Li Demei, won an international trophy at the Decanter World Wine Awards, launching Ningxia's international reputation.

history.title: Peak and pivot
history.text: Chinese wine production peaked at more than 13 mhl; that year an anti-corruption campaign curbed lavish banquets and gifts, and consumption began a long decline.

history.title: Ningxia classification and Ao Yun
history.text: Ningxia introduced a classification of Helan Mountain East estates (expanded to five tiers in 2016); LVMH's Ao Yun made its first vintage high in Yunnan.

history.title: EU-China GI agreement
history.text: The EU-China agreement on geographical indications came into force on 1 March 2021, protecting Chinese wine names including Helan Mountain East Foothill, Yantai, Shacheng and Huanren Icewine in the EU.

history.title: OIV World Congress in Ningxia
history.text: Ningxia hosted the 46th OIV World Congress of Vine and Wine in Yinchuan from 12 to 18 October 2026, a sign of its status as China's flagship region.

country.classification:
China's wine GIs are protected under national systems (the former AQSIQ geographical-indication product scheme, now run by the China National Intellectual Property Administration), with production standards for named areas such as 'Helan Mountain East Foothill' (贺兰山东麓葡萄酒), 'Yantai' (烟台葡萄酒), 'Shacheng' (沙城葡萄酒), 'Changli' (昌黎葡萄酒) and 'Huanren Icewine' (桓仁冰酒). Four of them (Helan Mountain East Foothill, Yantai, Shacheng and Huanren Icewine) are protected in Europe under the EU-China agreement in force since March 2021. Boundaries are generally administrative and not published as precise maps, so in this atlas they appear as points.

Ningxia also runs China's only official estate classification. Introduced in 2013, when ten wineries became Fifth Growths, it was expanded in 2016 to five tiers (Fifth to First Growth) and is reviewed every two years by a panel of experts, with First Growths to be re-examined every ten years. By 2021 nine estates had reached Second Growth (including Helan Qingxue, Kanaan, Chateau Hedong, Legacy Peak, Lisi and Chateau Yuquan) and the First Growth tier was still empty. Beyond that, labels rely on producer reputation; much Chinese wine carries no regional claim at all.
country.climate_soils: China's wine regions sit in two very different climates. The north and west (Ningxia, Xinjiang, Gansu, Inner Mongolia, Hebei's Huailai basin, Shanxi) are continental and dry, with hot summers, abundant sun and very cold winters, so vines are buried each autumn; irrigation from the Yellow River, Tianshan snowmelt or underground water is essential. Soils are typically sandy and gravelly alluvial fans (Helan Mountain East) or loess. The east coast (Shandong's Jiaodong Peninsula, coastal Hebei, Beijing, Tianjin) is warmer in winter but has a summer monsoon that brings humidity and disease just as grapes ripen. The south-west mountains of Yunnan and Sichuan offer a third option: high valleys at 2,000 to 2,600 m, sheltered from the monsoon by the Himalayan rain shadow, where Ao Yun and its neighbours grow Cabernet Sauvignon on river terraces.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: The dominant wine grape, the core of Ningxia's and Xinjiang's best reds.

grapes.name: Marselan
grapes.note: A 1961 French cross of Cabernet Sauvignon and Grenache, introduced in 2001, now promoted as a Chinese signature for its colour, softness and mildew resistance.

grapes.name: Cabernet Gernischt (Carmenère)
grapes.note: Imported by Changyu in the 1890s and long thought to be a Cabernet Franc relative; DNA profiling showed it is Carmenère. Common in Shandong.

grapes.name: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Petit Verdot
grapes.note: Widely planted in Ningxia, Hebei and Xinjiang.

grapes.name: Chardonnay, Riesling, Italian Riesling (Welschriesling)
grapes.note: The main whites; Italian Riesling was planted extensively in the 1950s to 1980s.

grapes.name: Vitis amurensis and hybrids (Beibinghong, Shuangyou)
grapes.note: Cold-hardy native and hybrid grapes in Jilin and Liaoning used for 'mountain grape' wines and icewine; Vidal is used at Huanren.

grapes.name: Rose Honey (Mei Gui Mi)
grapes.note: A heritage table-and-wine grape planted by French missionaries in Yunnan in the nineteenth century, still made into wine at Mile.

Jeannie Cho Lee, Mastering Wine for the Asian Palate

regions.name: Ningxia
regions.tagline: A desert strip between the Yellow River and the Helan Mountains that became China's showcase for fine wine.
regions.summary: Ningxia's vineyards run for about 200 km along the alluvial fans at the eastern foot of the Helan Mountains, between the mountains and the Yellow River, from Shizuishan in the north through Yinchuan, Yongning and Qingtongxia to Hongsipu. With about 40,400 ha (606,000 mu) of vines and 131 wineries in 2026, the Helan Mountain East Foothill area claims nearly 40 percent of China's estate vineyard. Its Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Marselan reds and its Chardonnay whites have won hundreds of international medals since Helan Qingxue's 2011 Decanter trophy.
regions.history: Changyu and Great Wall planted grapes here in the 1980s and shipped them east for winemaking. The provincial government turned arid land into a wine zone from the late 1990s, and boutique wineries (Helan Qingxue, Silver Heights, Kanaan, Domaine Pushang, Chateau Yuanshi) emerged in the 2000s. Moët Hennessy's Chandon Ningxia (2013) and Pernod Ricard's Helan Mountain winery followed, and the region launched China's only estate classification in 2013. It hosted the OIV World Congress in October 2026.
regions.terroir: A high (about 1,100 to 1,200 m), arid, continental climate with about 200 mm of annual rain, 3,000 hours of sunshine, hot summer days and very cold winters (minus 20 degrees C or lower), so every vine is buried in November. Soils are gravelly, sandy alluvial fans washed down from the Helan Mountains; irrigation comes from the Yellow River.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Marselan, Cabernet Gernischt, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling.
regions.styles: Bordeaux-style reds, Marselan, Chardonnay, traditional-method sparkling (Chandon).
regions.classification: National GI Helan Mountain East Foothill (protected in the EU); Ningxia's five-tier winery classification (2013, expanded 2016, reviewed every two years).

regions.name: Xinjiang
regions.tagline: China's largest wine-grape province, oasis vineyards on the old Silk Road between the Tianshan and the deserts.
regions.summary: Xinjiang, in China's far west, has the country's largest area of vineyards, most of them for table grapes and raisins (Turpan is famous for both). Wine vineyards cluster in three areas: the northern foothills of the Tianshan around Changji, Manas and Shihezi; the Yanqi Basin by Bosten Lake near Korla (Hoxud and Yanqi counties); and the Turpan depression, one of the hottest and lowest places in Asia. CITIC Guoan's Suntime, Tiansai, Chateau Zhongfei and Xinjiang Changyu (Baron Balboa) are notable producers.
regions.history: Grapes have grown in Xinjiang's oases for over 2,000 years; the Tang learned winemaking from Gaochang near Turpan in 641. Large state farms planted wine grapes from the 1970s; boutique estates such as Tiansai (Yanqi, 2010) and Puchang (Turpan) arrived in the 2010s.
regions.terroir: Extreme continental desert climate with very hot summers, freezing winters (vines buried) and less than 100 mm of rain in places; irrigation from Tianshan snowmelt via canals and karez (qanat) tunnels. Sandy and gravelly soils.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Marselan, Syrah, Chardonnay, Riesling, Saperavi.
regions.styles: Ripe, sun-drenched reds; some sweet and fortified wines.
regions.classification: No EU-protected wine GI; Yanqi and Tianshan North are promoted as producing areas; Turpan and Hoxud were proposed as national GIs in 2015.

regions.name: Shandong
regions.tagline: The cradle of modern Chinese wine, on a monsoon-lashed peninsula between two seas.
regions.summary: Shandong's Jiaodong Peninsula, around Yantai, Penglai and Qingdao, is where China's modern wine industry began with Changyu in 1892. It remains a major production centre, with hundreds of wineries and the headquarters of Changyu, although many big companies also process grapes and imported bulk wine here. Penglai's hills, near the coast, have attracted Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Long Dai, first vintage 2017) and boutique estates.
regions.history: Zhang Bishi's Changyu (1892), the Grand Cellar beneath Yantai (1894 to 1905), Huadong winery near Qingdao (1985, an early producer of Chardonnay), and later Long Dai and Chateau Changyu-Castel.
regions.terroir: Maritime-influenced and milder in winter, so vines need not be buried; but the summer monsoon brings heavy rain in July and August, making disease control the main challenge. Granitic and sandy soils on hillsides near Penglai.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Gernischt, Merlot, Marselan, Chardonnay, Petit Manseng, Italian Riesling.
regions.styles: Light to medium reds, whites, some sweet Petit Manseng.
regions.classification: National GI Yantai (protected in the EU); Penglai is promoted as a sub-zone.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Hebei
regions.tagline: Two very different wine areas: the dry Huailai basin beyond the Great Wall, and the coastal Changli hills.
regions.summary: Hebei's Huailai County (with Shacheng, Great Wall's home) lies in the Sanggan River valley north-west of Beijing, behind the Great Wall, where a dry, windy, sunny climate suits red grapes and Dragon's Eye (Longyan) table grapes have grown for centuries. Huailai is also home of the Sino-French demonstration vineyard (2001, now Domaine Franco-Chinois) that introduced Marselan. Changli, on the Bohai coast near Qinhuangdao, is the other major area. Grace Vineyard's sister estate and Chateau Sungod (Huailai) are among its boutique producers.
regions.history: Great Wall winery was founded at Shacheng in 1983 and made China's first dry white in 1979 as a state research project. Changli's Huaxia Great Wall winery (1988) and the Sino-French vineyard made Hebei a centre of experimentation.
regions.terroir: Huailai: continental, dry (about 400 mm of rain) and cold in winter, vines buried. Changli: maritime, milder, monsoon rain in summer.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Marselan, Chardonnay, Longyan (Dragon's Eye).
regions.styles: Reds and dry whites; Longyan whites.
regions.classification: National GIs Shacheng (protected in the EU) and Changli.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Yunnan
regions.tagline: Vineyards at 2,000 to 2,600 m in Tibetan valleys under the Meili Snow Mountains.
regions.summary: In north-west Yunnan, along the upper Mekong (Lancang) and Jinsha (upper Yangtze) rivers in Deqin and Shangri-La counties, small terraced vineyards sit between 2,000 and 2,600 m. French Catholic missionaries planted vines at Cizhong church in the nineteenth century; LVMH's Ao Yun, after a four-year search by Australian winemaker Tony Jordan, released its first Cabernet blend (2013) in 2016, and Shangri-La Winery and smaller estates followed. Further south, Mile and Mengzi grow the old Rose Honey grape.
regions.history: Missionaries at Cizhong kept vines for mass wine until their expulsion in 1952; Catholic villagers continued to tend them. The government encouraged villagers to plant vines in the 1990s, and Moët Hennessy contracted 320 small plots in 2012 for Ao Yun.
regions.terroir: High altitude, dry valleys in the rain shadow of the Himalayas, strong UV, cool nights; river-gravel and schist soils. Different villages ripen weeks apart because of altitude and sun exposure.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Syrah, Petit Verdot, Chardonnay, Rose Honey.
regions.classification: No national wine GI; Deqin and Shangri-La are promoted as producing areas.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Gansu
regions.tagline: Vineyards along the Hexi Corridor, the Silk Road route between desert and the Qilian Mountains.
regions.summary: The Hexi Corridor runs for 1,000 km through Gansu between the Qilian Mountains and the Gobi, through Wuwei, Zhangye and Jiayuguan. Grapes were grown at Liangzhou (Wuwei) in the Tang dynasty, whose wine the poets praised. Today Mogao, Ziyuan and Qilian wineries farm vines buried every winter.
regions.history: Liangzhou grape wine was famed in the Tang; modern plantings date from the 1980s and 1990s.
regions.terroir: Arid, continental, high (1,400 to 1,800 m); snowmelt irrigation; loess and gravel.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling.
regions.styles: Reds, whites and some icewine-style sweet wines.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)

regions.name: Shanxi
regions.tagline: Loess plateau country, home of Grace Vineyard, one of China's first boutique estates.
regions.summary: Grace Vineyard at Taigu, founded by Hong Kong businessman C.K. Chan in 1997, was one of the first Chinese estates to win international attention for quality, with wines such as Chairman's Reserve; his daughter Judy Leissner ran it for many years. Taiyuan was famous for grape wine in the Tang dynasty.
regions.history: Taiyuan's 'mare's teat' grape wine was a Tang dynasty luxury; Grace Vineyard revived the area's reputation from 1997.
regions.terroir: Continental loess plateau at about 800 m; vines buried in winter.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Beijing
regions.tagline: Capital-region wineries in the Yanqing and Fangshan hills.
regions.summary: Vineyards in Yanqing, north-west of the city beyond the Great Wall, and in Fangshan to the south-west support a cluster of chateaux aimed at Beijing's market and tourists, including Bodega Langes and Chateau Changyu AFIP in Miyun.
regions.history: Small plantings since the 1990s and a government push for 'wine chateau' tourism in the 2000s.
regions.terroir: Continental, monsoon summer rain, cold winters.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

regions.name: Liaoning
regions.tagline: Icewine on Hanlong Lake, near the North Korean border.
regions.summary: In Huanren County, Liaoning, the area around Hanlong Lake has cold winters but enough sun to ripen Vidal, and since the early 2000s Changyu and others have made icewine from grapes frozen on the vine. Huanren Icewine is a GI protected in the EU.
regions.history: Vidal was introduced from Canada; Changyu built its Golden Icewine Valley at Huanren.
regions.terroir: Cold continental climate; lake moderates temperatures; vines buried or protected.
regions.classification: National GI Huanren Icewine (protected in the EU).

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026)
EU-China Agreement on Geographical Indications (in force 1 March 2021), list of Chinese GIs

cn-changli.name: Changli
cn-changli.summary: A coastal producing area near Qinhuangdao on the Bohai Sea, protected as a national GI. It holds the Huaxia Great Wall winery, whose Cabernet was one of China's first serious varietal reds.
cn-changli.terroir: Sandy soils near the coast; maritime climate with summer monsoon rain.

cn-helan-mountain-east-foothill.name: Helan Mountain East Foothill
cn-helan-mountain-east-foothill.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Marselan, Cabernet Gernischt, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling
cn-helan-mountain-east-foothill.summary:
China's best-known wine GI, covering the gravelly alluvial fans along the eastern foot of the Helan Mountains in Ningxia, from Shizuishan through Yinchuan's Xixia district, Yongning and Qingtongxia to Hongsipu. In 2026 it had about 606,000 mu (40,400 ha) of vines and 131 wineries, by its own count nearly 40 percent of China's estate vineyard. The GI was among four Chinese wine names protected in Europe when the EU-China agreement came into force in March 2021.

The region's rise has been rapid. The provincial government reclaimed desert for vineyards from the late 1990s, and small estates arrived in the 2000s: Silver Heights (Emma Gao, trained in Bordeaux), Helan Qingxue (whose Jiabeilan 2009, made with consultant Li Demei, won a Decanter international trophy in 2011), Kanaan, Domaine Pushang, Chateau Yuanshi and Chateau Hedong. Big groups followed: Changyu built Chateau Changyu Moser XV with Austrian Lenz Moser, Great Wall built Tianfu, and Moët Hennessy opened Chandon Ningxia for sparkling wine in 2013. The region's five-tier estate classification, begun in 2013, has nine Second Growths as of 2021 and no First Growth yet.

The wines are typically ripe but fresh Bordeaux blends and Cabernet Sauvignon, with polished tannins, plus Marselan, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. The challenge is the climate: winters reach minus 20 degrees C or colder, so vines are buried under soil from November to April, which limits vine age and adds cost.
cn-helan-mountain-east-foothill.terroir: Altitude about 1,100 to 1,200 m; roughly 200 mm of annual rain and 3,000 hours of sun; large day-night temperature swings. Gravelly, sandy alluvial fans with some loess, low in organic matter; irrigation from the Yellow River.
cn-helan-mountain-east-foothill.nerd_note: Burying vines each winter means many Ningxia vineyards are trained with a slanted trunk ('crawling' or 'Ningxia-style' training) so the vine can be bent over and covered with soil.

cn-hexi-corridor.name: Hexi Corridor
cn-hexi-corridor.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling
cn-hexi-corridor.summary: A narrow Silk Road corridor through Gansu between the Qilian Mountains and the Gobi, through Wuwei (ancient Liangzhou, whose wine Tang poets praised), Zhangye and Jiayuguan. Modern vineyards, buried each winter, supply wineries such as Mogao and Ziyuan.
cn-hexi-corridor.terroir: Arid, continental and high (1,400 to 1,800 m); snowmelt irrigation; loess and gravel.

cn-huanren-icewine.name: Huanren Icewine
cn-huanren-icewine.summary: A GI for icewine from Huanren County in Liaoning, near the North Korean border, where grapes (mostly Vidal) are left on the vine to freeze and pressed while frozen, concentrating sugar and acid. Changyu's Golden Icewine Valley on Hanlong Lake is the best-known producer. It is one of four Chinese wine GIs protected in the EU.
cn-huanren-icewine.terroir: Cold continental winters with a moderating lake; vineyards at about 380 m.

cn-shacheng.name: Shacheng
cn-shacheng.grapes: Longyan (Dragon's Eye), Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay
cn-shacheng.summary: The GI for the Huailai basin around Shacheng town in Hebei, north-west of Beijing behind the Great Wall, along the Sanggan River and Guanting Reservoir. The state-owned Great Wall winery (founded 1983, now COFCO) is based here, and the area's centuries-old Longyan (Dragon's Eye) grape makes its traditional dry white. Newer estates such as Chateau Sungod and Great Wall Sanggan produce Bordeaux-style reds, and the Sino-French demonstration farm of 2001, now Domaine Franco-Chinois, brought Marselan to China.
cn-shacheng.terroir: Dry, sunny and windy valley at about 500 m; cold winters require vine burial; sandy loam soils.
cn-shacheng.nerd_note: Great Wall's dry white made from Longyan in the late 1970s, the result of a state research project, is usually cited as China's first modern dry white wine.

cn-shangri-la-deqin.name: Shangri-La (Deqin)
cn-shangri-la-deqin.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Syrah
cn-shangri-la-deqin.summary: High valleys of the upper Mekong and Jinsha rivers in Deqin County, under the sacred Meili Snow Mountains, where small vineyards at 2,200 to 2,600 m produce China's most expensive wine, LVMH's Ao Yun, a Cabernet-led blend first released (2013 vintage) in 2016. French missionaries first planted vines at Cizhong church in the nineteenth century.
cn-shangri-la-deqin.terroir: Dry valleys in the Himalayan rain shadow, strong sun, cold nights; river gravel and schist. Villages ripen weeks apart because of altitude and aspect.

cn-tianshan-north-foothills.name: Tianshan North Foothills
cn-tianshan-north-foothills.summary: Vineyards along the northern foothills of the Tianshan around Changji, Manas and Shihezi, including CITIC Guoan's Suntime and Xinjiang Changyu's Baron Balboa estate. Large state-farm plantings from the 1970s supply both big brands and newer estates.
cn-tianshan-north-foothills.terroir: Continental desert with hot summers and severe winters; alluvial soils; snowmelt irrigation.

cn-turpan.name: Turpan
cn-turpan.grapes: Thompson Seedless, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay
cn-turpan.summary: The Turpan depression, partly below sea level and one of the hottest places in Asia, has grown grapes for over 2,000 years; its raisins and seedless table grapes are famous throughout China. The Tang dynasty learned winemaking here after conquering Gaochang in 641. A small modern wine industry includes Loulan and Puchang; Turpan was proposed for national GI protection in 2015.
cn-turpan.terroir: Extremely hot, arid depression (summer highs above 45 degrees C), irrigated by karez underground canals; sandy soils.

cn-yanqi-basin.name: Yanqi Basin
cn-yanqi-basin.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Marselan, Merlot, Riesling, Chardonnay
cn-yanqi-basin.summary: A basin on the southern side of the Tianshan near Bosten Lake and Korla, at about 1,000 to 1,200 m, which since the 2010s has become Xinjiang's leading quality area. Tiansai Vineyards and Chateau Zhongfei make structured, sunny reds. Hoxud County, in the basin, was proposed as a national GI in 2015.
cn-yanqi-basin.terroir: Desert continental climate, gravel and sandy soils, Tianshan snowmelt irrigation; vines buried in winter.

cn-yantai.name: Yantai
cn-yantai.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Gernischt, Merlot, Marselan, Chardonnay, Petit Manseng
cn-yantai.summary: The GI for wine from Yantai on the Jiaodong Peninsula, the birthplace of modern Chinese wine. Zhang Bishi founded Changyu here in 1892 and dug its Grand Cellar beside the sea. Today Yantai (with the Penglai district) has the largest concentration of wineries in China, from Changyu's headquarters and its Chateau Changyu-Castel to Domaines Barons de Rothschild's Long Dai in the Qiushan valley. Its maritime climate spares vines from burial but brings monsoon rain at harvest, so wines are typically lighter and fresher than Ningxia's.
cn-yantai.terroir: Hilly, granite- and sand-based soils near the Bohai and Yellow Sea; mild winters, humid summers.
cn-yantai.nerd_note: Changyu's Cabernet Gernischt, a grape it imported in the 1890s, turned out on DNA testing to be Carmenère, which also went unrecognised in Chile until 1994.

sites.name: Jiahu
sites.text: A Neolithic village in Wuyang County, Henan, occupied from about 7000 to 5700 BC. Chemical analysis of residues in its pottery jars, published by Patrick McGovern and colleagues in 2004, found a fermented drink of rice, honey and fruit, probably including hawthorn and wild grape: the oldest chemically confirmed alcoholic beverage in the world. The site is also famous for bone flutes.

sites.name: Changyu Wine Culture Museum and Grand Cellar
sites.text: Changyu's original site in Yantai, founded by Zhang Bishi in 1892. The Grand Cellar, built from 1894 and finished after being rebuilt three times, lies seven metres underground and less than 100 metres from the sea; it still holds large oak casks. The museum tells the story of the company and of Chinese wine.

sites.name: Chateau Changyu-Castel
sites.text: A French-style chateau built by Changyu with France's Castel group at Beiyujia near Yantai, with about 135 ha of vineyards. Its signature grape is Cabernet Gernischt, the variety Changyu imported in the 1890s that DNA later showed to be Carmenère.

sites.name: Long Dai
sites.text: Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite) chose the Qiushan valley near Penglai for its Chinese estate in 2008, building terraces on granite hillsides. The first vintage of Long Dai, a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Marselan and Cabernet Franc, was 2017.

sites.name: Great Wall Sanggan Estate, Shacheng
sites.text: COFCO's Great Wall, China's largest wine brand, was founded at Shacheng in the Huailai basin in 1983; its Sanggan estate on the Sanggan River makes the company's top reds. The basin, behind the Great Wall north-west of Beijing, is dry, windy and sunny.

sites.name: Silver Heights
sites.text: Emma Gao, who studied in Bordeaux, and her father Gao Lin founded Silver Heights at the foot of the Helan Mountains; their first vintage was 2007. Its The Summit red helped show that Ningxia could make fine, balanced Bordeaux blends, and the estate is a reference for the region.

sites.name: Helan Qingxue
sites.text: A small Ningxia estate whose Jiabeilan 2009, made with consultant Li Demei, won an international trophy at the 2011 Decanter World Wine Awards, putting Ningxia on the international map. It is one of the region's Second Growths.

sites.name: Chateau Changyu Moser XV
sites.text: A large chateau built by Changyu with Austrian winemaker Lenz M. Moser near Yinchuan, opened in 2013. In 2013 its wines were listed by London's Berry Bros. & Rudd, the first Chinese chateau wines carried by the merchant.

sites.name: Kanaan Winery
sites.text: Wang Fang's Kanaan winery in Ningxia's Xixia district, founded in the early 2010s, makes Bordeaux blends and Riesling and was promoted to Second Growth in the regional classification.

sites.name: Chandon Ningxia
sites.text: Moët Hennessy's Chandon opened its Chinese sparkling-wine winery at the foot of the Helan Mountains in 2013, after Australian winemaker Tony Jordan chose Ningxia for its dry climate.

sites.name: Ao Yun
sites.text: LVMH's estate in Deqin County, Yunnan, whose name means 'flying above the clouds'. After Australian winemaker Tony Jordan spent four years searching China for a site, Moët Hennessy signed a joint venture in 2012 and leased 320 small plots across four villages at 2,200 to 2,600 m. The first vintage, 2013, was released in 2016. Each village ripens at a different time because of altitude and sun.

sites.name: Cizhong Catholic Church
sites.text: A church on the upper Mekong in Deqin County, built by French missionaries, where vines (including a variety thought to be Rose Honey) were planted in the nineteenth century for mass wine. After the missionaries were expelled in 1952, Catholic villagers kept the vineyard and still make wine.

sites.name: Grace Vineyard
sites.text: Founded in 1997 by Hong Kong businessman C.K. Chan at Taigu in Shanxi, Grace Vineyard was one of the first Chinese boutique estates to gain international recognition. His daughter Judy Leissner ran it for years; its Chairman's Reserve is a Bordeaux-style blend.

sites.name: Tiansai Vineyards
sites.text: A boutique estate in the Yanqi Basin of Xinjiang, founded in 2010, at about 1,100 m near Bosten Lake. It became one of the best-known Xinjiang wineries, with Cabernet, Marselan and whites.

sites.name: Turpan grape valley
sites.text: Turpan's Grape Valley, in one of the hottest depressions on earth, has grown grapes for more than 2,000 years, irrigated by karez underground canals that carry snowmelt from the Tianshan. The Tang learned their 'method of wine making' from nearby Gaochang in 641.

sites.name: Huanren Icewine (Hanlong Lake)
sites.text: On Hanlong Lake in Huanren County, Liaoning, Changyu and others make icewine from Vidal grapes frozen on the vine. The lake moderates temperatures so that grapes can hang into December without being destroyed.

sites.name: Yinchuan (OIV Congress 2026)
sites.text: Ningxia's capital Yinchuan hosted the 46th OIV World Congress of Vine and Wine in October 2026,. The city is the hub of the Helan Mountain East Foothill wine region, whose vineyards run along the desert edge west of town.
